vignette:
She is 58, a North American woman who has been widowed for several years, and when she begins telling her story it always starts with her husband's last ordinary morning. She remembers the sound of the kettle and the way he stood at the counter in his work boots, teasing her for misplacing her glasses when they were on her head. Nothing in that morning feels dramatic in retrospect, and that is part of what haunts her. She had gone out later to run errands, thinking about bills and whether she should start looking for part-time work again after a long stretch of unemployment. By the time she got the phone call, the world had already split into a before and an after.

Her husband had been injured in a violent accident. She does not like saying more than that at first. She says only that other people reached him before she did, that strangers saw what no wife should see, and that by the time she arrived at the hospital she was already too late in the ways that mattered. She still remembers details she does not want: the smell of antiseptic, the fluorescent lights, the way a doctor's mouth kept moving while she could not make sense of any words. She recalls looking at her husband's hands because she could not bear to look at his face. Even now, years later, she wakes with those hands in her mind, still and unfamiliar.

In the first months after his death, she moves through practical tasks as if she is impersonating a competent person. She signs forms, answers casseroles at the door, and thanks people for flowers she does not remember receiving. At night she lies down exhausted but cannot sleep. The moment the house quiets, images break through-hospital corridors, a ringing phone, his empty chair. Sometimes she drifts off only to wake in panic, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that she has missed another call and that something terrible is happening again. She begins leaving lights on in the hallway and television noise in the living room because silence feels dangerous.

Before he died, she had imagined unemployment as temporary, an uncomfortable chapter before she reentered work. Afterward, even simple responsibilities become unmanageable. She tries updating her resume one afternoon at the kitchen table, but the blank screen and the pressure to summarize herself make her chest tighten. She cannot concentrate long enough to finish a paragraph. If an employer leaves a voicemail, she listens to it repeatedly without calling back. The thought of being expected somewhere, of making small talk, of pretending to be steady, feels impossible. Over time she stops describing herself as "between jobs" and starts saying, with flat embarrassment, that she is not working.

As the years pass, her life narrows. She avoids the road that leads to the hospital. She cannot tolerate sirens; when she hears them, her body reacts before her mind does, her shoulders locking and her stomach dropping as if bad news is coming specifically for her. She keeps her phone on loud at all times but resents it when it rings. Unexpected calls make her hands shake. She stops attending neighborhood barbecues because someone always asks about her husband or tells her she is "so strong." In the grocery store she studies exits, abandons carts when she feels overwhelmed, and sometimes leaves without the things she came for.

She knows other people expect grief to soften into memory. What troubles her is how present everything remains. She does not simply remember what happened; she reenters it. A smell in a waiting room, the sight of work boots by a door, even a certain quality of late afternoon light can pull her backward so suddenly that for a moment she is no longer a 58-year-old woman in a pharmacy or on her porch, but a wife hearing catastrophic news and trying to understand it. When that happens she feels ashamed afterward, as if she should have better control over herself by now.

She lives alone now in the house they shared, though she uses only a few rooms regularly. His jacket still hangs in the closet. Some days she takes it out just to feel close to him; other days the sight of it is unbearable. She talks to him while washing dishes or folding laundry, then catches herself and goes quiet. Sleep remains broken. She checks the locks repeatedly before bed and startles at small sounds. Her memory has become unreliable in daily ways that frustrate her-misplaced keys, missed appointments, conversations she cannot fully recall because part of her is always scanning for danger.

What she misses most is not only her husband, but the version of herself that existed before that phone call: a woman who could plan ahead, laugh easily, and imagine a future. Now her days are organized around getting through rather than looking forward. She tells herself each morning to do one practical thing-pay a bill, answer an email, take out the trash-and sometimes that is all she can manage. She is not confused about the fact that her husband died years ago. What she struggles with is that her body and mind still live as though the worst moment of her life is happening, or about to happen, all over again.
